content.content:
5:FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.
57:The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.
61:FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

# FIG. 4 - Enlarged section of the perimeter member end

**View:** Enlarged fragmentary section through the lower end of the perimeter member shown in FIG. 2, taken where the clearance is present, with the bedded layers beneath. Outline line work, hatching on cut material. The artwork is line work alone; apart from the view legend and sheet number, the only characters are the listed reference numerals and their leader lines. The view legend reads FIG. 4, below the drawing and clear of all line work.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet shows the perimeter member 24, drawn as one upright hatched column, and three hatched bands beneath it, and nothing more. The column is shown schematically as a plain upright rectangle, hatched throughout as one body. Its sides run straight and unbroken from the upper limit of the drawing area, where the column is broken off, down to the horizontal line closing its bottom, its hatching continuing whole between them.

The column stands over the left-hand part of the drawing area and is narrower than the bands beneath it, so that a wide open stretch of the top edge line of the uppermost band lies to the right of the column and is not overhung by it.

The three hatched bands lie one above another across the lower part of the drawing area, each spanning its full width and meeting the next along a straight horizontal boundary: the uppermost band is the covering element 36, the middle band is the bonding material 40, and the lowest band is the substrate 42. Between the bottom line of the column and the top edge line of the uppermost band lies open unhatched space, the two lines standing plainly apart and nowhere touching.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The perimeter member 24 is the whole hatched column. Identified well inside the hatching of that column, above the line closing its bottom.
- The bearing face 26 is the flat lower end face of the column, seen edge on as the single horizontal line closing the bottom of the column. Identified on that line itself, within the width of the column.
- The clearance 34 is that open unhatched space. Identified well inside it, touching neither of the two lines that bound it.
- The covering element 36 is the uppermost band. Identified well inside its hatching.
- The exposed face 38 is the upper face of the uppermost band, seen edge on as its top edge line. Identified on the open stretch of that top edge line lying to the right of the column.
- The bonding material 40 is the middle band. Identified well inside its hatching.
- The substrate 42 is the lowest band. Identified well inside its hatching.

All four sheet failures are addressed, and everything stays synchronized.

**Numeral 24 on FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 (rejected endpoint clusters).** In both perspective views the perimeter member is an edge-on band under the slab, so its only interior target was a thin strip that kept failing endpoint inspection. I moved numeral 24 off both perspective sheets onto the three views where the part has a large, unambiguous interior: FIG. 2 (hatched leg), FIG. 3 (ring band) and FIG. 4 (hatched column). Per the redistribution rule, the numeral and the canonical part name are now entirely absent from both briefs, and the structure remains only as context, described generically as an unnumbered band round the underside of the slab, with the band alone touching the tile. The Brief Description was synchronized: the FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 sentences no longer list the perimeter member among the parts shown schematically. No Detailed Description sentence claimed the perimeter member was visible in either view, so nothing else needed changing, and no numeral definition, part or specification text was deleted.

**FIG. 3 anchor clearance of 11.4 units.** The ring band was specified only as "of even width", which the renderer drew narrow. The two closed lines are now spaced widely apart so the band is a broad continuous surface, and the endpoint sits deep inside it with clear space on both sides before either edge is reached.

**FIG. 4 column position.** The brief demanded the column stand over the left-hand part of the drawing area, which is a rendering constraint with no basis in the disclosure. I removed it: the column need only be much narrower than the bands beneath it so a wide open stretch of the uppermost band's top edge line lies to its right, which is what the exposed face 38 endpoint needs. A centered column now conforms.

**Numeral 36 on FIG. 5.** Its target was pinned to the strip below the sagging pulling element. It now reads simply as the open expanse of tile to the left of the machine, clear of the machine, the pulling element and the tile outlines.

Coverage after redistribution: every one of the 16 numerals still appears on at least one sheet, per-sheet counts are 6, 6, 2, 7 and 3, and all five briefs are under 2800 characters.

input.summary: Repaired all four failing sheets through the figure briefs alone. Numeral 24 was redistributed off the two perspective views, where the perimeter member appears only as a thin edge-on band that kept producing rejected endpoint clusters, onto FIG. 2, FIG. 3 and FIG. 4, where the part has a large interior. Its numeral and canonical part name were removed entirely from the FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 briefs, the structure remaining as an unnumbered band for context, and the FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 sentences of the Brief Description were synchronized. The FIG. 3 ring band is now specified as broad with its two closed lines spaced widely apart, and the numeral 24 endpoint sits deep inside it with clearance from both edges. The FIG. 4 requirement that the column stand over the left-hand part of the drawing area was removed as an invented rendering constraint; the column need only be much narrower than the bands so a wide open stretch of the uppermost band's top edge line lies to its right. The numeral 36 target on FIG. 5 was widened from the strip below the pulling element to the open expanse of tile to the left of the machine. No claim, numeral definition, disclosed part or specification passage was deleted; all 16 numerals still appear on at least one sheet, per-sheet counts are 6, 6, 2, 7 and 3, and every brief is under 2800 characters.
reasoning: Numeral 24 failed on FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 for a structural reason, not a wording one. In a perspective view the perimeter member is an edge-on band beneath the slab, so the only interior target it offers is a thin strip; every endpoint placed there lands close to a line and the marked-endpoint check rejects the cluster. Two earlier turns had already tried to buy clearance with wording ('the band is deep enough for its front surface to read plainly'), and it failed again, which told me the target region itself was the problem.

Rather than keep demanding a deeper band (an invented proportion adopted purely to control the renderer, and effectively a demand for label room), I used the redistribution route the figure-plan rules provide: numeral 24 now appears on FIG. 2, FIG. 3 and FIG. 4, each of which gives it a genuinely broad interior, being respectively a hatched leg, a ring band and a hatched column. Nothing was deleted; the numeral simply lives on the sheets that can carry it.

Redistribution obliged me to strip both the numeral and the canonical name from the old briefs, not just the label. Both perspective briefs now describe the structure generically as a band running round the underside of the slab with the band alone touching the tile, and each says expressly that the band carries no reference numeral on that sheet. Keeping the band as unnumbered context preserves the disclosed relationship that the base stands clear of the covering element while the perimeter contacts it.

Synchronization ran one way only, from text to figures. The Brief Description had said the perimeter member was shown schematically in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, so those two sentences were trimmed. I checked the Detailed Description first: no sentence there places the perimeter member in either view (it cites FIG. 3 for the closed loop, and FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 for the lower end and clearance), so no description text needed touching and none was lost.

FIG. 3 failed on clearance because the brief specified the band only as 'of even width', which left the renderer free to draw it thin, and 11.4 units is what a thin band yields. Width here is a pure depiction convention, not a disclosed proportion, so widening it costs the invention nothing: the two closed lines are now spaced widely apart, the band is a broad continuous surface, and the endpoint is targeted deep inside it with clear space on both sides. I gave no numeric width, which would have been invented.

FIG. 4 was the clearest case of over-specification. 'The column stands over the left-hand part of the drawing area' is a rendering constraint with no source in the disclosure, and the renderer centered the column instead. The correct repair is to drop the constraint, not to fight the renderer or to adopt the drawn position as though it meant something. What the sheet actually needs is that the column be much narrower than the bands so a wide open stretch of the uppermost band's top edge line lies to its right for the exposed face 38 endpoint; a centered column satisfies that, so the brief now requires only that and states that no particular horizontal position is required.

Numeral 36 on FIG. 5 was constrained to the tile surface 'below the flexible pulling element 46', which is a narrow wedge between a sagging curve and the tile outline. I replaced it with the whole open expanse of tile to the left of the machine, clear of the machine, the pulling element and the tile outlines, using an explicit left/right term rather than a positional relationship to a curved line.

I verified coverage after the move rather than assuming it: all 16 numerals still appear on at least one sheet, no sheet exceeds eight, and the briefs run 2425, 2724, 2139, 2790 and 2436 characters. Removing two bullets also bought length headroom on the two perspective sheets.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged by this turn; no claim, description passage or citation was touched, and the repairs were confined to figure briefs plus the two Brief Description sentences that named parts no longer numbered on those sheets. Claim 1 still rests on a rigid low-friction perimeter member terminating in a bearing face that leaves a clearance along at least part of its length through which ambient air enters continuously, an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric under that continuous ingress, an all-rigid vibration path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed, and a bearing face slidable while the pressure differential is maintained. The non-sealing clearance and the no-elastomer path carry it clear of DE-202021002652-U1, whose suction cup is a rubber-elastic apron lying in the vibration path, and of US-11408462-B2, whose peripheral wall is elastic partitions with a rigid frame added only to stop them being drawn inward. Simultaneous holding and sliding carries it clear of US-10001245-B2, where vacuum suction and frictionless air-cushion movement are alternative modes of one generator. Delivering vibration into the covering element across a maintained rigid contact carries it clear of US-4934475-A, where vibration imparts a lifting force that reduces the suction-adhering force so the body walks along the wall. US-11247858-B2 remains uncited because its reproduced passages describe a perforated suction plate and sweeping nozzle bar and support no statement about a low-friction or non-sealing perimeter. Moving numeral 24 between sheets changes nothing about what the perimeter member is or does in the claims and description.

# FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, onto the covering element 36. Outline line work, no shading or hatching, every line solid. The artwork is line work alone; apart from the view legend and sheet number, the only characters are the listed reference numerals and their leader lines. The covering element 36 is one large plain tile filling the lower part of the drawing area. The machine stands on the left-hand part of that tile, leaving a wide open expanse of tile surface to the right of it. The machine is a slab, the base 12, carrying two separate closed housings on its top face and a grip above them, and standing on a band round its underside, the band alone touching the tile. Slab, housings, grip and band are all shown schematically. The band carries no reference numeral on this sheet.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The vibration motor 18 is the left-hand of the two housings on the base 12, its front face a plain uninterrupted surface. Identified well inside that front face.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is the right-hand of the two housings on the base 12, its front face likewise plain and uninterrupted. Identified well inside that front face.
- The handle 44 is a simple grip carried on the machine above the base 12 and clear of the two housings, drawn as one closed outline enclosing a visible open area, a depiction convention only that asserts no particular handle form. Identified on the drawn outline of the grip, clear of the housings and the base 12, and not in the open area it encloses.
- The covering element 36 is that large plain tile. Identified well inside the open expanse of tile surface to the right of the machine, clear of the machine and the tile outlines.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile, as in FIG. 1, filling the lower part of the drawing area. The machine stands on the right-hand part of that tile, leaving a wide open expanse of tile surface to the left of it. The machine is a plain slab carrying two separate closed housings and standing on a band that runs round the underside of the slab, the band alone touching the tile; slab, housings and band are all shown schematically. The band is drawn with generous visible depth, so that the stretch of its front surface facing the viewer reads as a broad open strip between the underside of the slab and the tile, wide enough from its upper to its lower edge line to take an endpoint deep inside it.

It meets the outer silhouette of the vibration device 10, that meeting place being shown schematically, then runs away to the left across the open tile, sagging gently, and is broken off well inside the left-hand limit of the drawing area, running throughout as one simple open curve. - The covering element 36 is that large plain tile, on which the machine stands. Identified well inside the open expanse of tile surface to the left of the machine, clear of the machine, of the flexible pulling element 46 and of the tile outlines.

The mismatch is resolved.

**Declaration/sheet-list mismatch on FIG. 1 and FIG. 5.** Both files carried numeral 24 in their `## Numerals shown on this figure` list while the `**Numerals appearing on this figure:**` declaration line omitted it, so the two records of the same sheet disagreed. I reconciled them in favour of keeping the perimeter member labelled on both perspective views:

- FIG. 1 declaration now reads 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44, matching its list.
- FIG. 5 declaration now reads 10, 24, 36, 46, matching its list.
- Both briefs carry a numeral 24 bullet again, identifying the perimeter member as the band under the slab running round the underside at its edge, targeted deep inside the band's front surface on the long stretch facing the viewer, clear of its upper and lower edge lines.
- Each geometry paragraph now specifies that the band is drawn with generous visible depth so its front surface reads as a broad open strip between the underside of the slab and the tile, which is what gives that endpoint room. The earlier statements that the band carried no numeral on those sheets are gone.

The Brief Description already listed the perimeter member among the parts shown schematically in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, so it matches the restored briefs without further change.

Restoring the bullets pushed both files over the length limit, so I trimmed the new depth sentence and the new endpoint sentence in each: FIG. 1 is 2768 and FIG. 5 is 2776, with all five briefs under 2800. Numeral 24 now appears on all five sheets, per-sheet counts are 7, 6, 2, 7 and 4, the 16-entry table is unchanged, and no claim, description passage or numeral definition was touched this turn.

input.summary: Fixed the mechanical preflight failure: the FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 briefs each declared a numeral set that disagreed with their own sheet list, which still carried numeral 24. Both are reconciled by keeping the perimeter member labelled on the two perspective views. The FIG. 1 declaration now reads 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44 and the FIG. 5 declaration now reads 10, 24, 36, 46, each matching its list exactly. A numeral 24 bullet was restored to both briefs, identifying the perimeter member as the band under the slab and targeting an endpoint deep inside the band's front surface on the long stretch facing the viewer, clear of its upper and lower edge lines, and each geometry paragraph now gives the band generous visible depth so that front surface reads as a broad open strip. The statements that the band carried no reference numeral on those sheets were removed. The Brief Description already named the perimeter member as shown schematically in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, so it matches without change. Both files were trimmed after the restoration to stay within the length limit: FIG. 1 is 2768 and FIG. 5 is 2776, all five briefs under 2800. Numeral 24 now appears on all five sheets, per-sheet counts are 7, 6, 2, 7 and 4, and no claim, description passage, numeral definition or disclosed embodiment was altered.
reasoning: The failure was a records mismatch inside two files, not a rendering problem. Each figure brief states its numerals twice, once in the bold declaration line and once in the trailing list. On FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 the declaration omitted 24 while the list still contained it, so the preflight reported 24 as missing from the declaration. Only one of the two could be right, and the fix was to make them agree.

I reconciled upward rather than downward, restoring 24 to the declarations instead of stripping it from the lists. The Brief Description in draft/07-drawings.md names the perimeter member among the parts shown schematically in both FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, and it was already back in that state; had I removed 24 from the sheet lists I would have had to strip the text again to keep them synchronized. Keeping the numeral means the text stands as written and the label sits on the two views where the reader first meets the machine.

Restoring the label meant restoring a target it can actually occupy, since the earlier endpoint rejections on these two sheets came from the band being drawn as a thin edge-on strip. Both geometry paragraphs now give the band generous visible depth so its front surface reads as a broad open strip between the underside of the slab and the tile, and the bullet targets an endpoint deep inside that surface on the long stretch facing the viewer, clear of the upper and lower edge lines. Depth of the drawn band is a depiction convention on a schematic body, so specifying it adds nothing to the invention: the disclosure gives a rigid loop or skirt at the perimeter and says nothing about its proportions, and nothing about proportions entered the claims, description or numeral table.

The sentences saying the band carried no reference numeral on those sheets had to go with the restoration, since they now contradicted the declarations. That wording only ever existed to support the redistribution, which this gate has reversed.

Adding the bullets pushed FIG. 1 to 2962 and FIG. 5 to 2970 characters, over the 2800 limit, so I shortened the two sentences I had just added in each file rather than cutting established geometry. The endpoint still reads 'deep inside the front surface of the band, on the long stretch facing the viewer, clear of its upper and lower edge lines', which keeps the broad interior target and the clearance requirement in fewer words.

I checked the other three briefs for the same declaration-versus-list disagreement and found none: FIG. 2, FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 match on both records. Per-sheet counts after the restoration are 7, 6, 2, 7 and 4, all within the eight-numeral limit, and every one of the 16 defined numerals still appears on at least one sheet.

No text outside figures/ needed editing this turn. draft/07-drawings.md already carried the perimeter member in both sentences, the Detailed Description never tied that part to FIG. 1 or FIG. 5, and the claims, numeral table and description were left untouched.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged by this turn; the edits were confined to two figure briefs and touched no claim, description passage or citation. Claim 1 still rests on a rigid low-friction perimeter member terminating in a bearing face that leaves a clearance along at least part of its length through which ambient air enters continuously, an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric under that continuous ingress, an all-rigid vibration path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed, and a bearing face slidable while the pressure differential is maintained. The non-sealing clearance and the no-elastomer path carry it clear of DE-202021002652-U1, whose suction cup is a rubber-elastic apron lying in the vibration path, and of US-11408462-B2, whose peripheral wall is elastic partitions with a rigid frame added only to stop them being drawn inward. Simultaneous holding and sliding carries it clear of US-10001245-B2, where vacuum suction and frictionless air-cushion movement are alternative modes of one generator. Delivering vibration into the covering element across a maintained rigid contact carries it clear of US-4934475-A, where vibration imparts a lifting force that reduces the suction-adhering force so the body walks along the wall. US-11247858-B2 remains uncited because its reproduced passages describe a perforated suction plate and sweeping nozzle bar and support no statement about a low-friction or non-sealing perimeter. Giving the drawn band visible depth is a depiction convention on a schematic body and adds no proportion, structure or embodiment to the application text.

When a tile or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.

Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place. In one known hand-held device for lifting and laying tiles, a handle carries two shafts, an electric motor vibrates the shafts, and a head shell at the free end of each shaft carries a suction cup on its underside, the suction cups being evacuated by an electrically operated pump and each being formed by a rubber-elastic apron [REF:DE-202021002652-U1].

Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.

The same reliance on a compliant wall, and the same treatment of holding and moving as alternatives, are found in vacuum coupling arrangements used away from tile setting. In one adhesion device that holds itself to a wall surface, the peripheral wall of the decompressed space between the base and the wall surface is formed by elastic partitions whose ends contact the wall surface, and a frame member of higher rigidity is added on the partition to restrict the partition from being deformed into that space as it is drawn down [REF:US-11408462-B2]. In a base assembly for coupling an end effector to a structure, a cavity on the second side of the assembly is held to the structure by vacuum drawn by a pneumatic generator operating in a suction mode, and the assembly is moved across the structure substantially frictionlessly on an air cushion produced by the same generator operating in a blower mode [REF:US-10001245-B2], so that the vacuum coupling is given up for the period during which the assembly is moved. In a device that suction-adheres to a wall surface and moves along it, a seal member mounted in the main body defines a pressure reduction space in cooperation with the wall surface, vacuum creating means discharges fluid from that space so that the main body adheres by the difference in fluid pressure inside and outside the space, and vibration generating means mounted on the main body imparts a lifting force in a direction away from the wall surface that reduces the suction-adhering force, together with a force along the wall surface that moves the main body [REF:US-4934475-A]. The vibration there is spent on loosening the hold and driving the body along the surface, rather than being delivered into the surface as the working output of the tool.

The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles reduce some of the vibration reaching the operator, but they do so by absorbing mechanical energy that would otherwise have gone into the covering element, so the tool is made kinder to the operator by being made worse at its job. The two problems are coupled: firmer coupling to the covering element is obtained by pressing harder, and pressing harder is exactly what increases the vibration dose to the operator.

What is needed is a way to hold a vibration device against a covering element with a force that does not come from the operator's arms, to conduct the vibration into the covering element without passing it through any compliant member, and to allow the device to be moved from area to area over the covering element without ever giving up that hold.

The single finding is fixed.

**Background overstatement of US-11408462-B2.** The sentence attributed wall-surface contact to the elastic partitions generally, while the record recites two partitions with different roles: the first sits on the fringe of the base and forms only the base-side portion of the peripheral wall, and it is the second, disposed nearer the wall surface, whose wall-surface-side end contacts the wall surface. The sentence now reads that the peripheral wall "is formed by elastic partitions, of which the partition nearer the wall surface has an end that contacts the wall surface". The rest of the sentence, including the higher-rigidity frame member restricting the partition from being deformed into the decompressed space, and the citation token, are unchanged.

Nothing else was touched. The paragraph's point is unaffected, since what carries the invention clear of that reference is the compliant peripheral wall itself rather than which partition touches the wall. The three other characterizations in the same paragraph were confirmed accurate against their records by the review and were left alone.

All five figure briefs remain unchanged and under 2800 characters, the numeral table and every figure declaration are untouched, and the draft is free of em dashes, notes, placeholders and questions.

input.summary: Corrected the one verified finding, a single clause in the Background's characterization of US-11408462-B2. The text had said the peripheral wall of the decompressed space "is formed by elastic partitions whose ends contact the wall surface", which attributes wall contact to both partitions. The record recites the first partition on the fringe of the base forming only the base-side portion of the peripheral wall, and the second partition, disposed nearer the wall surface, whose wall-surface-side end contacts the wall surface. The clause now reads "is formed by elastic partitions, of which the partition nearer the wall surface has an end that contacts the wall surface". The remainder of the sentence, including the higher-rigidity frame member restricting the partition from being deformed into the decompressed space as it is drawn down, and the citation token, are unchanged. No other file was edited: the figure briefs, numeral table, claims, Summary, Detailed Description and Brief Description are all as they were, all five briefs remain under 2800 characters, and the draft carries no em dash, note, placeholder or question.
reasoning: The finding was accurate against the reference file. US-11408462-B2 recites two elastic partitions doing different jobs: the first is disposed on a fringe of the base and forms the base-side portion of the peripheral wall, while the second is disposed closer to the wall surface side and it is that partition whose wall-surface-side end contacts the wall surface. Writing 'elastic partitions whose ends contact the wall surface' credited the reference with a contact relationship it does not recite for the base-side partition.

I took the reviewer's wording because it is the minimal accurate correction and keeps the sentence's grammar and the citation placement intact. An inaccurate characterization of cited art is worth fixing on its own terms, quite apart from any gate: it is the kind of thing that gets quoted back during prosecution.

The correction costs the paragraph nothing argumentatively. What distinguishes this invention from that reference is that the peripheral wall is compliant at all, and that the rigid frame member there exists only to stop the elastic partition being sucked into the decompressed space, which is the opposite of a rigid member that transmits vibration. Which of the two partitions touches the wall does not bear on that contrast, so narrowing the clause leaves the Background's point standing.

I confined the edit to the clause named in the finding. The review had checked the other half of the same sentence and the characterizations of DE-202021002652-U1, US-10001245-B2 and US-4934475-A against their records and found them accurate, so re-touching them would risk introducing an error into text already verified.

No figure, numeral, claim or description text is implicated by a Background prior-art characterization, so nothing needed synchronizing. I confirmed the five briefs are unchanged and still within the length limit, and that the draft remains free of notes, placeholders and questions.

The deliberate non-sealing clearance and the no-elastomer path carry it clear of DE-202021002652-U1, whose suction cup is a rubber-elastic apron lying in the vibration path between the vibrated shaft and the tile. They also carry it clear of US-11408462-B2, whose peripheral wall is formed by elastic partitions, the one nearer the wall surface making the contact, with a higher-rigidity frame member added only to stop that partition being drawn into the decompressed space; that reference keeps the compliant wall rather than replacing it. Simultaneous holding and sliding carries claim 1 clear of US-10001245-B2, where vacuum suction and substantially frictionless air-cushion movement are alternative modes of the same pneumatic generator. Delivering vibration into the covering element across a contact the hold never releases carries it clear of US-4934475-A, where the vibration imparts a lifting force that reduces the suction-adhering force so the main body walks along the wall. US-11247858-B2 remains uncited because its reproduced passages describe a perforated suction plate with a sweeping nozzle bar and support no statement about a low-friction or non-sealing perimeter. This turn's edit only made the US-11408462-B2 characterization narrower and more exact, so no argument built on the Background was widened.

All five sheets are addressed in their briefs.

**FIG. 1, spurious line work.** The renderer added a vertical seam splitting the band's front strip, paired bead/flange contours around the slab, and a stepped edge implying a second layer under the tile. The brief now forbids each explicitly: the tile is drawn with single edge lines and no step, ledge or further layer along any edge; every face of the slab is bounded by single edge lines with no bead, flange, rim or paired parallel contour; and the band's front surface is one broad open strip that no vertical, seam or joint line crosses anywhere along its length. These are line-work restrictions on bodies the brief already specified, so no structure was added.

**FIG. 2, numeral 14.** The endpoint landed a pixel inside the hatching rather than on the slab's upper edge line. The first side is a face seen edge-on, so a line is the only correct target; the bullet now states that the endpoint sits on that upper edge line itself, touching the line and not in the hatching below it, on a stretch clear of the housing.

**FIG. 3, sheet-edge frame.** The outer rectangle was drawn flush to the page margins and read as a border, with the inner rectangle offset. The brief now requires the ring to occupy the middle of the drawing area and stand well in from every side, with a wide expanse of empty paper between the outer rectangle and each limit of the drawing area, and states that no border, frame or other line follows or approaches the sheet edges. The inner rectangle is now specified as concentric, evenly spaced from the outer on all four sides, so the band is of equal generous width all the way round.

**FIG. 4, numeral 26.** The bearing face is the line closing the column's bottom, which was too short a target. The column is now drawn broad so that bottom line is a long, plainly visible segment, while still narrower than the bands so the open stretch numeral 38 needs remains to its right. The endpoint must touch that bottom line, away from its two ends, and sit neither in the hatching above nor the space below.

**FIG. 5, numeral 24.** Same band treatment as FIG. 1: generous visible depth, one uninterrupted front strip crossed by no seam or joint line, with the endpoint well inside that strip clear of its upper and lower edge lines.

Adding these constraints pushed four files past 2800 characters, so I compressed the boilerplate view sentence and other redundant phrasing on each sheet. All five now run 2435 to 2793 characters, every declaration still matches its sheet list, and no claim, description passage, numeral definition or drawing description was changed.

The sheet shows one rectangular ring and nothing else. The ring is the perimeter member 24 seen end on: a closed band with a rectangular opening through it, shown schematically with a rectangular plan outline, this being a depiction convention for this sheet only.

The machine stands on the right-hand part of that tile, leaving a wide open expanse of tile to the left. The machine is a plain slab carrying two separate closed housings and standing on a band round its underside, the band alone touching the tile; slab, housings and band are shown schematically. Every face of the slab is bounded by single edge lines, with no bead, flange, rim or paired parallel contour.

The band is drawn with generous visible depth, its front surface reading as one broad open strip between the underside of the slab and the tile. That strip is uninterrupted: no vertical, seam or joint line crosses it anywhere along its length.

The flexible pulling element 46 runs away to the left across the open expanse of tile. The place at which it meets the machine is shown schematically, no particular attachment location or attachment formation being shown.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

content.text:
All five sheets are addressed.

**FIG. 1, stepped base, rim, and shared 10/44 coordinates.** The slab is now specified as a simple box drawn thick, its top face one flat unbroken surface, with no rim, lip, step, bead or paired parallel contour on or around it. The two colliding endpoints are now driven apart by geometry rather than by wording: numeral 10 sits on the silhouette where it runs down the left-hand side face of the slab, well below the grip, and numeral 44 sits on the grip outline high above the slab. The grip itself is specified as carried well above the slab.

**FIG. 2, numeral 14.** The first side is a face, and in a vertical section it can only appear as an edge-on line, which is why the endpoint kept landing inside the hatching across two providers. I moved numeral 14 to FIG. 1, where the same face is a broad visible surface: it is now identified well inside the top face of the slab, clear of the housings and the grip, while numeral 12 moves to the slab's broad front face so the two stay distinct. Numeral 14 and the term "first side" are gone from the FIG. 2 brief. No text ties the first side to a particular figure, so nothing in the Brief Description, Detailed Description or numeral table needed changing.

**FIG. 3, third rectangle.** The brief now states that the finished sheet carries two closed rectangular lines and no third, that the opening inside the inner rectangle holds no further rectangle, border or centre line, and that the band itself carries no line of its own.

**FIG. 4, closed column top and stray marks.** The column is now expressly cut off at the upper limit of the drawing area, with no line closing it across the top, so its only horizontal line is the one closing its bottom. Each band carries plain even hatching and nothing else, with no stray dot, curl or speck.

**FIG. 5, doubled cord.** The pulling element is now one unbroken curved stroke of even thickness, one line and not two, with no second line beside it and no interior between lines.

FIG. 1 now carries eight numerals, which is the per-sheet maximum; all sixteen numerals still appear on at least one sheet, every declaration matches its list, and the five briefs run 2451 to 2795 characters. The claims, description, drawing descriptions and numeral table are unchanged.

input.summary: Repaired all five sheets in their briefs. FIG. 1: the slab is now a simple box drawn thick with one flat unbroken top face and no rim, lip, step, bead or paired parallel contour, and the colliding endpoints for numerals 10 and 44 are separated by geometry, 10 on the silhouette down the left-hand side face of the slab well below the grip, 44 on the grip outline high above the slab. FIG. 2: numeral 14 kept landing inside the hatching because the first side can only appear as an edge-on line in section, so it moved to FIG. 1, where that same face is a broad visible surface; numeral 12 moved to the slab's broad front face to stay distinct, and both numeral 14 and the term first side are gone from the FIG. 2 brief. FIG. 3: the sheet must now carry two closed rectangular lines and no third, with no further rectangle, border or centre line inside the opening and no line on the band itself. FIG. 4: the column is expressly cut off at the upper limit with no line closing it across the top, and each band carries plain even hatching with no stray dot, curl or speck. FIG. 5: the pulling element is one unbroken curved stroke, one line and not two, with no second line beside it and no interior. No text tied the first side to a particular figure, so the claims, description, drawing descriptions and numeral table are unchanged. FIG. 1 now carries eight numerals, the per-sheet maximum; all sixteen numerals appear on at least one sheet, every declaration matches its list, and the briefs run 2451 to 2795 characters.
reasoning: Numeral 14 had now failed twice, the second time under cross-provider inspection with the dot 15 pixels below the line inside the base hatching. The root cause is structural: the first side is a face, and a vertical section can only show a face edge-on as a line, so the target is a one-dimensional feature that the endpoint placer keeps missing on the wrong side. A third attempt at tightening the same wording would have been the same experiment.

So I moved numeral 14 to FIG. 1, where the top face of the slab is a genuinely broad visible region, which is what the endpoint rules ask for. That forced a second decision: numeral 12 had been on that top face, so it moved to the slab's broad front face. The assignment is semantically right rather than merely convenient, because the first side is defined as the face turned away from the covering element, which is exactly the top face in that view, while the base is the whole slab and can be identified on any part of it.

I checked before moving that no text ties the first side to a particular figure. The Brief Description of FIG. 2 names the base, the chamber and the perimeter member, and the Detailed Description mentions the first side 14 four times without a figure reference. So the move needed no text change, and the numeral table entry is untouched.

The cost is that FIG. 1 now carries eight numerals, which is the cap. I considered dropping numeral 36 from that sheet to make room, but the tile is what the view is about, the Brief Description says the device is shown in use on a covering element, and its endpoint in the open expanse of tile has never been questioned. Eight within the limit is better than removing a label that works.

The FIG. 1 collision report, anchor endpoints sharing coordinates for 10 and 44, was really a geometry problem: the grip was specified only as carried above the base, so it could be drawn close over the housings, and an endpoint on the machine silhouette could coincide with one on the grip outline. Rather than describe the exclusion in words again, I put vertical distance between them, the grip carried well above the slab, 10 well below the grip on the slab's side face, 44 high above the slab on the grip outline.

The stepped base and raised rim on FIG. 1 were invented line work. The previous brief said only that faces are bounded by single edge lines with no bead, flange, rim or paired contour, which the renderer satisfied by drawing a stepped profile instead. Naming the body positively, a simple box with one flat unbroken top face, closes that gap, and saying it is drawn thick gives numeral 12 the broad front face it now needs.

FIG. 4 had two separate defects. The column drawn as a closed rectangle contradicts the fragmentary section it is meant to be, so the brief now states positively that no line closes it across the top and that its only horizontal line is the one closing its bottom. The stray curl and dot in the bonding material are noise, so each band is now required to carry plain even hatching and nothing else.

FIG. 3's third rectangle and FIG. 5's doubled cord are both cases of the renderer adding a stroke. For the cord I followed the rule that a pulling element is one curved path and must never be defined as a strip with an interior or by counting outline strokes, so the brief says one line and not two, with no interior between lines.

Adding all these constraints pushed FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 over the length limit, so I recovered the space from wording that carries no requirement: repeated phrases like 'of that column' and 'the two lines that bound it', and the redundant 'with the bedded layers beneath' in a view sentence that already names the bedded layers.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged by this turn; every edit was a line-work or endpoint constraint inside a figure brief, and no claim, description passage or citation was touched. Claim 1 still rests on a rigid low-friction perimeter member terminating in a bearing face that leaves a clearance along at least part of its length through which ambient air enters continuously, an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric under that continuous ingress, an all-rigid vibration path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed, and a bearing face slidable while the pressure differential is maintained. The deliberate non-sealing clearance and the no-elastomer path carry it clear of DE-202021002652-U1, whose suction cup is a rubber-elastic apron in the vibration path, and of US-11408462-B2, whose peripheral wall is formed by elastic partitions, the one nearer the wall surface making contact, with a higher-rigidity frame member added only to stop that partition being drawn into the decompressed space. Simultaneous holding and sliding carries it clear of US-10001245-B2, where vacuum suction and frictionless air-cushion movement are alternative modes of one generator. Delivering vibration into the covering element across a contact the hold never releases carries it clear of US-4934475-A, where vibration imparts a lifting force reducing the suction-adhering force so the body walks along the wall. US-11247858-B2 remains uncited because its reproduced passages describe a perforated suction plate and sweeping nozzle bar. Slab thickness, grip height, column width and the suppression of rims, seams, extra rectangles and doubled strokes are depiction conventions on schematic bodies and enter no claim or description; moving numeral 14 between sheets changes nothing about what the first side is.

invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,

disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet

or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

The declaration/list mismatch on both sheets is resolved.

**Numeral 14 belongs to FIG. 2.** The sheet lists are the authoritative numeral-to-sheet assignment, and they place the first side on FIG. 2, not FIG. 1. I aligned both files to them:

- FIG. 2 has its first side 14 bullet back, and its declaration now reads 12, 14, 20, 22, 24, 36, matching its list.
- FIG. 1 no longer declares 14, and its declaration reads 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44, matching its list. Numeral 12 returns to the broad visible part of the slab's top face, which the top face is free to carry again.

**Making that endpoint survive.** Since the first side stays on a sheet where it can only appear edge-on, I strengthened the geometry around it rather than the wording alone: the slab is now drawn thick, its upper edge line long, straight and plainly visible with a clear stretch to one side of the housing, and numeral 12 is pushed low into the hatching well clear of that line so the two cannot be confused. The endpoint for 14 must sit on the upper edge line itself with the terminal dot centred on the line so the line passes through it, which is the placement that tolerates a pixel of drift in either direction instead of failing when it drifts down into the hatching.

The FIG. 1 repairs from the last turn are kept: the slab is still specified as a simple box with one flat unbroken top face and no rim, lip, step, bead or paired parallel contour, and numerals 10 and 44 remain separated, 10 on the silhouette down the left-hand side face well below the grip and 44 on the grip outline high above the slab.

All five declarations now match their sheet lists, every numeral in the table appears on at least one sheet, per-sheet counts are 7, 6, 2, 7 and 4, and the briefs run 2584 to 2801 characters. No claim, description passage, drawing description or numeral definition was changed.

input.summary: Resolved the preflight mismatch by aligning both briefs to their sheet lists, which assign numeral 14 to FIG. 2 rather than FIG. 1. FIG. 2 has its first side 14 bullet restored and its declaration now reads 12, 14, 20, 22, 24, 36; FIG. 1 no longer declares 14 and reads 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44, with numeral 12 returned to the broad visible part of the slab's top face. Because the first side stays on a section view where it can only appear edge-on, the surrounding geometry was strengthened: the slab is drawn thick, its upper edge line long, straight and plainly visible with a clear stretch to one side of the housing, numeral 12 sits low in the hatching well clear of that line, and the numeral 14 endpoint must sit on the upper edge line itself with the terminal dot centred so the line passes through it. The FIG. 1 repairs from the previous turn are preserved: the slab is a simple box with one flat unbroken top face and no rim, lip, step, bead or paired parallel contour, and numerals 10 and 44 remain far apart. All five declarations now match their sheet lists, every numeral appears on at least one sheet, per-sheet counts are 7, 6, 2, 7 and 4, and the briefs run 2584 to 2801 characters. No claim, description passage, drawing description or numeral definition was changed.
reasoning: The report named both halves of one mismatch: numeral 14 was in the FIG. 1 declaration but not its sheet list, and in the FIG. 2 sheet list but not its declaration. That tells me the sheet lists are the authoritative numeral-to-sheet assignment held outside the brief text, and that my move of 14 from FIG. 2 to FIG. 1 last turn was not accepted. So the reconciliation had to run toward the lists, which put 14 back on FIG. 2.

That returns numeral 14 to a view where the first side can only be shown edge-on as a line, which is what caused the two earlier endpoint rejections. Since relocating the label is not available, I attacked the conditions that made the dot land wrong. The recorded failures were consistently a downward drift of one to fifteen pixels into the base hatching, so I required the terminal dot to be centred on the upper edge line with the line passing through it; a centred dot straddles the line and survives drift in either direction, where an endpoint merely aimed at the line fails as soon as it slips below.

I also gave that line room to be found. The slab is now drawn thick with a long, straight, plainly visible upper edge line and a clear stretch to one side of the housing, and numeral 12 was pushed low into the hatching well clear of that line. Previously 12 was targeted only 'well inside its hatching, clear of every drawn line', which left it free to sit just under the top edge and compete with 14 for the same neighbourhood.

content.text:
The flagged endpoint target is replaced with a broad one.

**FIG. 2, numeral 14.** The instruction "the terminal dot centred on the line so that the line passes through it" specified an exact placement, which is what the check rejected. The bullet now reads: "Identified on that upper edge line, anywhere along the clear stretch of it to one side of the air-extraction mechanism 20." That names the whole free length of the line as the target rather than a precise point on it, and the geometry paragraph still requires that line to be long, straight and plainly visible with a clear stretch to one side of the housing, so there is a wide region for the leader to land in.

I also removed the depth modifier that had crept into the neighbouring bullet: numeral 12 is now "well inside its hatching, clear of its upper edge line", dropping "low in the slab". That keeps the two endpoints apart without dictating how deep into the body the dot must sit.

Nothing else changed. FIG. 2 is now 2719 characters, its declaration and sheet list both still read 12, 14, 20, 22, 24, 36, the other four briefs are untouched and within the limit, and the claims, description, drawing descriptions and numeral table are as they were.

input.summary: Replaced the flagged exact endpoint target on FIG. 2. The numeral 14 bullet had required "the terminal dot centred on the line so that the line passes through it", which prescribes a precise placement; it now reads "Identified on that upper edge line, anywhere along the clear stretch of it to one side of the air-extraction mechanism 20", naming the whole free length of the line as the target region. The geometry paragraph still requires that upper edge line to be long, straight and plainly visible with a clear stretch to one side of the housing, so the target remains wide. I also dropped the depth modifier from the adjacent numeral 12 bullet, which now reads "well inside its hatching, clear of its upper edge line" instead of "low in the slab and well clear of its upper edge line", keeping the two endpoints distinct without dictating how deep the dot sits. FIG. 2 is now 2719 characters, its declaration and sheet list both read 12, 14, 20, 22, 24, 36, the other four briefs are untouched, and no claim, description passage, drawing description or numeral definition was changed.
reasoning: The rejected phrase was one I added last turn to defeat a downward drift of the endpoint into the base hatching. It worked as a description of a pixel outcome, which is exactly why it reads as an arbitrary exact target: it told the placer where the dot must sit rather than which part it must mark. Replacing it with the whole clear stretch of the upper edge line gives a broad region and leaves the placer free within it.

I kept the geometry that supports the target rather than the wording that over-specified it. The slab is still drawn thick with a long, straight, plainly visible upper edge line and a clear stretch to one side of the housing, which is what makes a broad target on that line viable at all; that sentence describes the drawing, not a coordinate.

The neighbouring numeral 12 bullet carried 'low in the slab', which is the same kind of depth modifier the endpoint rules ask to remove and which nothing in the disclosure grounds. Dropping it while keeping 'clear of its upper edge line' preserves the only thing that separation actually needs, which is that 12 not crowd the line belonging to 14.

I checked the other four briefs for comparable phrasing before deciding whether to touch them. FIG. 4's numeral 26 says 'away from its two ends' and FIG. 3's numeral 24 says 'deep inside that band', but both name a region rather than a point, both are needed to keep the dot off a corner or an edge, and neither was flagged, so I left them rather than churning specifications that passed.

No application text is implicated by an endpoint instruction, and no numeral moved, so the Brief Description, Detailed Description, claims and numeral table needed no synchronization. I confirmed the FIG. 2 declaration still matches its sheet list and that all five briefs remain within the length limit.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged by this turn; the edit was confined to two endpoint sentences in one figure brief and touched no claim, description passage or citation. Claim 1 still rests on a rigid low-friction perimeter member terminating in a bearing face that leaves a clearance along at least part of its length through which ambient air enters continuously, an extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric under that continuous ingress, an all-rigid vibration path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed, and a bearing face slidable while the pressure differential is maintained. The deliberate non-sealing clearance and the no-elastomer path carry it clear of DE-202021002652-U1, whose suction cup is a rubber-elastic apron in the vibration path, and of US-11408462-B2, whose peripheral wall is formed by elastic partitions, the one nearer the wall surface making contact, with a higher-rigidity frame member added only to stop that partition being drawn into the decompressed space. Simultaneous holding and sliding carries it clear of US-10001245-B2, where vacuum suction and frictionless air-cushion movement are alternative modes of one generator. Delivering vibration into the covering element across a contact the hold never releases carries it clear of US-4934475-A, where vibration imparts a lifting force reducing the suction-adhering force so the body walks along the wall. US-11247858-B2 remains uncited because its reproduced passages describe a perforated suction plate and sweeping nozzle bar. Where a leader endpoint lands is a drawing matter and enters no claim or description.
